Like for like

An AI agent migrated 2 legacy features. A harness checked 1,136 records against the original. Every difference stopped for a human decision.

A work sample for a migration tech lead role. Moving a feature with an agent is the easy half; this page is about the other half: what the harness has to prove, where the agent must stop for a person, and how tenant isolation is tested.

Legacy source: a simulated OutSystems application, moved to multi-tenant PostgreSQL.

  • Real run output
  • Tenant token is a local stand-in for Cognito

Human gates the agent cannot skip

  • Only a human edits the triage file: it is write-protected for the agent.
  • The agent cannot read the original logic: 417 tool calls audited, 0 leaks.
  • The agent cannot change the harness, the legacy side or the platform schema.
  • A new dependency is a stop-and-ask, not an install.

Said plainly

The stops are real: each migration session ended and waited at those points. The decisions were proposed by a builder session (Claude) and reviewed and approved by the owner, Arthur Gao; run reports and knowledge entries written before that review keep their original wording. In a client project these decisions belong to the product owner and the tech lead.

3 things this run found past the happy path

Totals can match while records are wrong

With a deliberately wrong calculation, every tenant total still matched the original: the hour gained on one clock-change night was lost on the other. Only the per-employee weekly totals (4 of 192 weeks) and the record-by-record check (4 shifts) caught it. Comparing totals is not validation.

See the evidence

A lesson from the first feature was wrong for the second

The first migration left a rule for local times that occur twice. In the second feature the legacy system does the opposite. The agent followed the rule, the harness flagged the record, and the choice went to a person instead of being settled silently by either side.

See the evidence

Guardrails are enforced and audited, not promised

The agent worked without the original logic: 417 tool calls audited afterwards, 0 leaks. 16 calls were stopped by the guard, false positives included and listed. What the agent may not touch is write-protected, not just written in a prompt.

See the evidence

The evidence, in detail

The original: OutSystems-style tables and a calculation nobody may read

Simulated OutSystems data source. The legacy side is modelled on the physical tables an OutSystems application generates: OSUSR_<module>_<entity> table names, upper-case column names, DateTime values stored as local wall-clock time with no zone, soft delete through an IS_ACTIVE flag, and statuses kept as integer codes. The screen logic is a PostgreSQL function standing in for the OutSystems server action. The rows are synthetic, generated for this demo; nothing was exported from a real OutSystems environment, and this project is not affiliated with OutSystems.

3 tenants, 24 employees and 1,011 shifts, generated from a fixed seed. Start and end are stored as local wall-clock time with no zone; each tenant has a time zone. The legacy function legacy.fn_timesheet() returns paid hours and gross pay per payable shift. The migration session was denied read access to its source.

The brief, as the agent received it

Feature brief: Timesheet (hours and pay)

Written by the business analyst from the low-code "Timesheet" screen and its export.

What the screen does

Payroll staff open the Timesheet screen to see, for each shift that can be paid, the date it counts against, the paid hours and the gross pay. Payroll is run from this list, so the numbers must be exactly right to the cent.

Legacy data

Each tenant (customer company) has its own employees and shifts. Every tenant has a time zone (an IANA name such as Australia/Brisbane). Shift start and end are stored as the local time at the tenant, with no time zone attached.

CREATE TABLE legacy."OSUSR_A1B_TENANT" (
  "ID" integer PRIMARY KEY,
  "NAME" text NOT NULL,
  "TIMEZONE" text NOT NULL            -- IANA name
);

CREATE TABLE legacy."OSUSR_A1B_EMPLOYEE" (
  "ID" integer PRIMARY KEY,
  "TENANTID" integer NOT NULL,
  "FULLNAME" text NOT NULL,
  "HOURLYRATE" numeric(8,2) NOT NULL,
  "IS_ACTIVE" boolean NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE legacy."OSUSR_A1B_SHIFT" (
  "ID" integer PRIMARY KEY,
  "TENANTID" integer NOT NULL,
  "EMPLOYEEID" integer NOT NULL,
  "STARTDATETIME" timestamp NOT NULL, -- local wall-clock time, no zone
  "ENDDATETIME" timestamp NOT NULL,   -- local wall-clock time, no zone
  "BREAKMIN" integer NULL,            -- NULL = not recorded
  "STATUS" integer NOT NULL,          -- 1 draft, 2 approved, 3 paid
  "IS_ACTIVE" boolean NOT NULL        -- false = soft-deleted
);

Status codes: 1 draft, 2 approved, 3 paid. IS_ACTIVE = false on a shift means it was deleted on the screen (the row is kept).

Business rules

  1. Which shifts are payable. Only shifts that are not deleted and whose status is approved or paid. Whether the employee is still active does not matter: past shifts of a person who has left are still payable.
  2. Hours worked. Hours worked are the time between the start and the end of the shift.
  3. Break. If a break was recorded, use it (a recorded 0 means no break). If no break was recorded, take 30 minutes when the hours worked are more than 5 hours, otherwise no break.
  4. Paid hours. Hours worked minus the break, rounded to the nearest quarter hour. Exactly halfway rounds up.
  5. Gross pay. Paid hours times the employee's hourly rate, rounded to the cent. Exactly half a cent rounds up.
  6. Work date. The local calendar date on which the shift started.

What to deliver

Migrate every legacy row (tenants, employees and all shifts, including drafts and deleted ones) into the new model in platform/schema.sql, and rebuild the screen's calculation on it.

FileWhat it does
mapping.mdField-by-field mapping, every assumption, every open question
migrate.tsExports migrate(pool) (type MigrateFn in harness/contracts.ts). Reads legacy, writes app and migration.id_map as the migrator role. Ids are deterministic (UUIDv5 from entity + legacy id) and rows are upserted, so a second run changes nothing.
calc.tsExports calculate(client, claims) (type CalculateFn). Runs inside withTenant; returns one TimesheetRow per payable shift of that tenant, decimals as text. A pure function does the arithmetic; the query feeds it.
calc.test.tsUnit tests for the rules above

Feature code uses only the pool or client it is handed: it does not open its own connections or read connection settings (the harness refuses to load code that does).

npm run migrate -- timesheet runs the migration; npm run harness -- timesheet compares the result with the legacy screen, shift by shift.

  2. Map

    Write features/<name>/mapping.md: a table mapping every legacy field to its new field (or

  3. Build

    Write migrate.ts, calc.ts and calc.test.ts in features/<name>/, following

  4. Migrate
  5. Validate
  6. After human triage

    Fix what was triaged as new-system-bug (and legacy-bug-keep: the new system must reproduce

  7. Record
    • For each lesson, write one file knowledge/<slug>.md in this format:

Rules in CLAUDE.md

  • You migrate one feature at a time using the migrate-feature skill.
  • Read knowledge/ before anything else. Apply every entry that is relevant and say which ones you applied.
  • The harness decides what passes. Never edit harness/, legacy/, platform/schema.sql or harness/triage.yaml.
  • Never weaken or delete a test to make it pass.
  • Stop and ask the human when: the harness reports a mismatch; a rule in the brief is ambiguous; anything touches tenancy, RLS, roles or money rounding.
  • Money and hours are decimals, never floats. Tenant id comes from token claims only.
  • One commit per step, message prefixed with the step name.

Calculation (TimesheetRow)

OutputSource
shift_id, tenant_id, employee_idnew uuids
work_datelocal calendar date (tenant time zone) of start_at
paid_hoursrules 2–4, two decimals
gross_payrule 5, two decimals

Payable: deleted_at IS NULL AND status IN ('approved', 'paid'), employee active ignored.

Assumptions

  • Hours worked is real elapsed time (end_at - start_at as instants), not the difference of the wall-clock readings. For a shift that spans a DST change (Pacific/Auckland, 5 Apr 2026 and 27 Sep 2026) the two differ by one hour; the harness will show whether legacy agrees.
  • Ambiguous local time (the repeated hour when DST ends) is read as the earlier instant (daylight offset); non-existent local time (the skipped hour when DST starts) is moved forward by the gap (luxon's behaviour). Neither can be checked before migrating: the session guard does not allow ad-hoc queries on legacy.
  • "More than 5 hours" compares the exact hours worked (before rounding) with 5 h, strictly.
  • Paid hours are rounded from exact seconds to the nearest 900 s (quarter hour), half up (towards +∞). Gross pay is computed from the rounded paid hours.
  • Half a cent rounds up (towards +∞); with positive hours and rates this is the usual half-up.
  • paid_hours and gross_pay are always formatted with two decimals ("8.00", "181.98").
  • Deletion time is unknown in legacy, so deleted_at records when the migration first saw the row deleted; only its NULL/non-NULL state carries meaning.

Open questions

None left open. Decided after run 001 (runs/001/decisions.md):

  • D1: a shift and its employee must belong to the same tenant. The schema now enforces this with the composite foreign key (tenant_id, employee_id) → app.employee (tenant_id, id); the migration still checks it so the error names the shift.
  • D2: negative paid time (a break longer than the shift, or an end before the start) is a data error. calculate refuses it with an error naming the shift and never pays a negative amount. The migration still copies such a row unchanged and does not "fix" it by adding a day. Paid time of exactly zero is not negative and pays 0.00.
  • D3: the DST assumptions above are confirmed as rules.

Run 001: 5 of 5 checks passed, 0 mismatches in 914 records

The agent got the feature right on the first run. Nothing was staged: the harness compared every payable shift with the legacy function and found no difference, in the Auckland tenant (which changes its clocks twice in the seeded windows) as well as in the Brisbane control. The seeded-fault panel shows the same harness catching a deliberately wrong calculation.

The decision: 3 open questions settled, 5 lessons written down

Decisions after run 001

Run 001 passed every check with no mismatches, so harness/triage.yaml stays empty. These are decisions on the open questions in features/timesheet/mapping.md and in the run 001 summary.

Proposed by the builder session (Claude). Reviewed and approved by Arthur Gao, the owner, on 2026-11-27. Records written before that review (run reports, knowledge entries) keep their original wording.

#QuestionDecisionWho changes what
D1app.shift did not guarantee that a shift and its employee belong to the same tenant.Accepted. A child row carries tenant_id and references its parent by (tenant_id, id).Builder: composite foreign key in platform/schema.sql and an isolation check ("shift pointing at another tenant's employee is rejected"), commit d77fbfc.
D2A break longer than the shift, or an end at or before the start, gives negative paid hours.A shift with negative paid time is a data error: the calculation refuses it with an error naming the shift; it is never paid as a negative amount. D3Hours worked across a clock change; which instant an ambiguous local time means.Confirmed as rules: hours worked are the real elapsed time between the two instants in the tenant's zone; a local time that occurs twice (clocks go back) is the earlier instant; a local time that does not exist (clocks go forward) moves forward by the gap.Migration agent: knowledge entries.

Migration ids are UUIDv5 of entity and legacy id; upserts skip unchanged rows and keep first-seen values

migration · runs 001-002, feature timesheet, lesson by the migration agent, recorded after the triage of run 001 by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner

Rule

Derive every new id as UUIDv5 of "<entity>:<legacy id>" under one fixed namespace, and write all rows in one transaction as set-based upserts (unnest arrays) that update only when a value differs (WHERE (...) IS DISTINCT FROM (...)). A value that legacy does not hold and the migration has to invent (for example deleted_at from an IS_ACTIVE flag) is set on the first run and kept on later runs. Validate legacy references (tenant, parent, status code, time zone) before writing, and fail with the legacy id.

Why, and how it is checked
Why

The harness runs the migration twice and compares checksums of app.* and migration.id_map. Using now() on every run, or random ids, would change data that did not change.

Check

harness idempotency check (row counts and md5 per table before and after a second run); features/timesheet/migrate.test.ts, describes "uuidv5" (RFC 4122 vector, deterministic per entity and id) and "shiftStatus" (unknown code refused).

Legacy wall-clock times become instants in the tenant zone; durations are real elapsed time

dates and time zones, migration · run 001, feature timesheet, triage by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner (decision D3)

Rule

Read a legacy timestamp without a zone as wall-clock time in the tenant's IANA zone and store it as timestamptz. A local time that occurs twice (clocks go back) is the earlier instant; a local time that does not exist (clocks go forward) moves forward by the gap. A duration is the real elapsed time between the two instants, never the difference of the wall-clock readings. A local date (work date) is taken in the tenant zone, never in UTC or the machine zone.

Why, and how it is checked
Why

The brief only said "time between start and end". Pacific/Auckland changes its clocks (5 Apr and 27 Sep 2026), so the two readings differ by an hour, and luxon and Postgres each resolve ambiguous times their own way unless the code chooses explicitly.

Check

features/timesheet/migrate.test.ts, describe "localToInstant" (repeated hour → earlier instant, skipped hour → forward); features/timesheet/calc.test.ts, "counts real elapsed time on the night clocks go back" and "is the local date the shift started, not the UTC date"; harness records check (work_date and paid_hours per shift).

Negative paid time is a data error; refuse it by name, never pay a negative amount

domain, pay calculation · run 001, feature timesheet, triage by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner (decision D2)

Rule

When inputs give a negative quantity that is paid (a break longer than the shift, an end before the start), the calculation throws an error naming the record. It never clamps the value and never emits a negative amount. The migration copies such a row unchanged and does not repair it (for example by adding a day). A quantity of exactly zero is valid and pays 0.00.

Why, and how it is checked
Why

The brief did not say what happens to such rows. Rounding would have turned them into negative or zero pay with no signal, and payroll is run from this list.

Check

features/timesheet/calc.test.ts, describe "timesheetRow: negative paid time is a data error (decision D2, run 001)" (three tests: break longer than the shift, end before the start, exactly zero still pays); a harness run lists any refused shift under calcErrors in report.json.

Round in the smallest integer unit, one rounding per stated rule, ties toward +infinity

money and hours arithmetic · runs 001-002, feature timesheet, lesson by the migration agent, recorded after the triage of run 001 by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner

Rule

Do money and hour arithmetic on BigInt in the smallest exact unit (milliseconds, quarter hours, cents), with one explicit half-up rounding (floor((2n + d) / 2d)) at each rounding step the brief states, in its order. For timesheets, round paid time to the quarter first, then multiply the rounded quarters by the rate in cents and round to the cent. Format with exactly two decimals ("8.00").

Why, and how it is checked
Why

The brief states two roundings in order (paid hours, then pay), and with that order and integer arithmetic the legacy totals matched to the cent across 914 shifts. Exact half-cent ties are common with quarter hours and two-decimal rates (7.25 h × 25.10 = 181.975 → 181.98). A float product, or a rounding that sends ties toward zero or to even, misses by a cent.

Check

features/timesheet/calc.test.ts, describes "computePay: rounding paid hours to the quarter (rule 4)" and "computePay: gross pay to the cent (rule 5)"; harness totals and records checks (hours and gross per tenant and per shift).

A child row references its parent by (tenant_id, id), so it cannot point across tenants

platform tenancy, schema · run 001, feature timesheet, triage by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner (decision D1)

Rule

Every tenant-owned child table carries its own tenant_id and references its parent with a composite foreign key (tenant_id, parent_id) → parent (tenant_id, id), backed by UNIQUE (tenant_id, id) on the parent. A migration still checks the pairing itself, so its error names the legacy row.

Why, and how it is checked
Why

Before the fix, app.shift referenced app.employee by id alone. A runtime write could pair a shift with another tenant's employee, and a calculation that joins on tenant_id would silently drop the row (missing pay, no error). RLS does not catch this, because each row on its own passes the policy.

Check

harness isolation check "shift pointing at another tenant's employee is rejected" (harness/checks/isolation.ts, also listed in platform/isolation.test.ts); features/timesheet/migrate.ts fails with "shift N: tenant X differs from employee tenant Y".

Lessons written after clock-events

Compute durations at the time precision legacy pays at; store and order at full precision

dates and time, pay calculation · run 003, feature clock-events, triage by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner (decision clock-minutes-only, legacy-bug-keep)

Rule

Before a duration feeds a paid quantity, reduce each time to the precision the legacy screen pays at (clock terminals: whole minutes, seconds dropped, truncated in the tenant's local time). Keep the stored instant at full precision and order events by it; the reduction belongs to the calculation, not the migration.

Why, and how it is checked
Why

The brief said only "the time between the clock-in and the clock-out". Clock events carry seconds, and on 9 of 222 pairs the seconds moved paid time across a quarter-hour boundary (for example 12:37:35-21:00:04 pays 8.00 h at whole minutes, 7.75 h with seconds). Payroll has always paid whole minutes, so the new system reproduces it.

Check

features/clock-events/calc.test.ts, describe "clockShiftRows: whole minutes only (triage clock-minutes-only, run 003)" (rounds up, rounds down, and ordering still uses the exact time); harness records and totals checks (run 004: 0 unexplained).

Reuse a feature's helpers by import; extract a shared module only when a third feature needs them

code structure, migration · run 003, feature clock-events, decision D4 by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner (runs/003/decisions.md)

Rule

A new feature imports the helpers of an earlier feature (newId, localToInstant, computePay from features/timesheet/) instead of copying them. It adds only what it needs, for example a new entity name in the Entity union. A shared module is extracted when a third feature needs the same helpers, so its shape comes from three users.

Why, and how it is checked
Why

Clock-events needed the same id derivation, wall-clock reading and pay rounding as timesheet. Copies would let the two features drift apart without the harness noticing, and a shared module shaped by two users would be a guess.

Check

features/clock-events/migrate.test.ts (ids equal newId('clock_event', …) from timesheet) and features/timesheet/migrate.test.ts, describe "uuidv5"; the harness idempotency check runs both migrations.

A confirmed time-zone rule is kept when another legacy screen differs; the difference is triaged per record until the owner decides

dates and time zones, triage · run 003, feature clock-events, triage by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner (decision clock-repeated-hour, acceptable pending the product owner)

Rule

A rule already confirmed for the platform (D3: a repeated local time is the earlier instant) is applied to every new feature, even when that feature's legacy screen resolves the time differently. The harness difference is triaged per record and named as an open question for the product owner; the agent does not change the rule, or special-case one feature, without a decision.

Why, and how it is checked
Why

The clock screen reads a clock-out at 02:30 on 2026-04-05 in Auckland (the repeated hour) as the later instant, so legacy pair 295 pays 5.00 h where the new system pays 4.50 h. Following legacy here would have quietly given clock events a different meaning of local time from timesheets.

Check

features/timesheet/migrate.test.ts, describe "localToInstant" ("reads the repeated hour when DST ends as the earlier instant"), which clock-events shares; features/clock-events/migrate.test.ts, describe "clockEventRow" (occurred_at of 02:30 on 2026-04-05 is the earlier instant); harness run 004 lists pair 295 under triage clock-repeated-hour and no other mismatch.

"Next event" rules run on live rows, per owner, ordered by time (never by id), in a pure function

domain, event pairing · runs 003-004, feature clock-events, lesson by the migration agent, recorded after the triage of run 003 by the builder session (Claude) on behalf of the owner

Rule

A rule that looks at the next or previous record (pair a clock-in with the next event) drops soft-deleted rows first, groups by the owner (employee), orders by the instant with a fixed tie-break, and is a pure function over the rows the query returns; the SQL does not order or pair. Each condition gets a test: deleted rows in between, late-entered rows (ids not in time order), another owner's rows at the boundary, and mixed UTC offsets.

Why, and how it is checked
Why

Legacy ids are not in time order, and the runtime role cannot see legacy ids, so ordering by id would silently pair the wrong events. Done this way, the pairing matched legacy on all 222 pairs in run 003 (no missing or extra rows); every mismatch was in the hours.

Check

features/clock-events/calc.test.ts, describes "pairEvents: which events count (rule 1)" and "pairEvents: pairs (rule 2)"; harness records check (no missing or extra pairs in runs 003 and 004).

◆ Seeded

Seeded fault: we broke it on purpose

To prove the harness itself works, it was run against a deliberately wrong calculation: Elapsed time taken as the plain difference of the two local timestamps. Every other rule is right. It reported 8 differences on 4 shifts, all on the nights the Auckland clocks change, and none in the Brisbane control. Every tenant total still matched: the same staff gained an hour on one clock-change night and lost it on the other, so a check on tenant totals alone would have passed. The per-employee weekly totals (4 of 192 weeks differ) and the record-by-record check caught it.
